summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web app that lets you hear our planet change. It takes real visualizations from the NASA Earth Information Center and the Scientific Visualization Studio (hurricanes, the ozone hole, CO₂, ocean currents, melting ice, glacier retreat, night lights and more) and reads every frame while the video plays. Each frame becomes sound in two layers. The first is a calm musical accompaniment generated from the image’s colours, brightness and motion. The second is the natural sound of the phenomenon itself, such as wind for a hurricane, ice cracking for Greenland or rain for El Niño, and its strength follows the actual data, frame by frame. When the phenomenon is weak the sound is quiet and low; when it is strong it gets loud and high.

The project makes NASA’s Earth science data accessible to people who are blind or have low vision. It also gives everyone a new, emotional way to understand climate change: you hear details the eye can miss. Every video has a full description, keyboard controls and a link to the same data in NASA Worldview, so curiosity can turn into exploration.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Jukebox presents 16 curated NASA visualizations as full-screen videos in four categories: Atmosphere, Oceans, Ice and Land. Videos are streamed through our own server proxy, which lets the browser read each frame’s pixels. A small copy of each frame (128×72) goes onto a canvas and is analyzed in real time:

  • Music layer: We pull seven features from each frame: dominant color, saturation, warmth, brightness, texture, left/right balance and motion. Pure, tested functions turn them into music:
    • Dominant color sets the key, following the circle of fifths.
    • Warm reds give minor chords (tension), and cool blues give major chords (calm).
    • Brightness opens up the timbre and raises the register.
    • Detail and motion speed up the arpeggios.
    • Each category has its own instrument and register.
  • Phenomenon layer: For each visualization, we measure the colours NASA uses to encode the data, such as the red of ice-mass loss, the purple of the ozone hole or the yellow of city lights. We calibrated each measure on the real video, using the 5th–95th percentile across all frames, so 0% is the calmest moment and 100% the most intense. That level drives volume, pitch and density together. You hear more raindrops, stronger gusts, more ice cracks, or a faster heartbeat for heat.
  • Exploring time: You can drag the video or press ←/→ to go back and forward in time, and the sound follows the year on screen.
  • NASA Worldview: A “See in Worldview” button opens NASA Worldview with the matching satellite layers, region and date.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Science communication: Pairing music with data makes climate change easier to remember and feel, for students, museums and the general public.
  • Exploration: The project links storytelling (SVS videos) to raw data (Worldview), so users can investigate on their own.
  • Inclusion: The site is in English and Portuguese, works on phones and needs nothing to install.

Tools and technologies

  • TypeScript, React 19 and TanStack Start (Vite), with Tailwind CSS and Radix UI.
  • Web Audio API: All sounds are synthesized live in the browser, with no recorded audio.
  • Canvas API reads the pixels of each frame.
  • WebGL draws the rotating 3D Earth with NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble textures (via NASA GIBS).
  • Vitest for unit tests of the frame→music and frame→phenomenon mapping.
  • NASA data: Scientific Visualization Studio, the Earth Information Center, NASA Worldview and GIBS.
  • Built with Lovable and Claude Code, with version control on GitHub.

Creativity
Most sonifications turn one number into one pitch. Earth Jukebox listens to the images the way a person looks at them. It combines a musical mood, taken from color and light, with a recognizable natural sound whose intensity comes from the real data. A hurricane sounds like wind, a glacier drips, and ozone loss pings like a sonar. The rotating Earth and its welcome sound make the first visit feel like arriving in space.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: Sounds follow calibrated data, not decoration. Every Worldview layer and date was checked against Worldview’s real configuration, and Landsat views use cloud-free dates.
  • Accessibility first: We added descriptions, keyboard shortcuts and panels that open on demand, so the screen is never cluttered.
  • Listening comfort: Sound is gentle by default, can be turned off with one tap (or M), and the welcome sound plays only on the first visit.
  • Browser limits: We dealt with CORS through a same-origin proxy and with autoplay rules (sound starts on the first tap or key press).
  • Clean structure: The data mapping is pure and tested, separate from the audio code, so new visualizations are easy to add.
